opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I've been thinking about a lot, and I think it's actually underappreciated how much the success of Transformers depends on the data having been pre-processed into the right form.

The way I like to frame it is that attention is really good at working with data where each individual token is already semantically meaningful. If you think about language, by the time you've run it through a tokenizer like BPE, each token roughly corresponds to a word or a sub-word, something that carries meaning on its own. Attention is essentially doing pairwise comparisons between all these units, building up a kind of exhaustive cache of everything it's seen. That's a great inductive bias when the units are meaningful, because comparing two words directly is a sensible operation.

But when you go to lower-level, more raw representations, say characters, bytes, raw audio samples, or individual pixels, each unit on its own doesn't mean much. A single audio sample at 16 kilohertz tells you almost nothing. In those settings, attention's strengths matter less, its quadratic cost really hurts because sequences get very long, and what you actually want is something that compresses information as it goes, building up higher-level abstractions from the raw signal. That's where I think recurrent-style models, like state space models, have a natural advantage, since they're built around maintaining a compressed state.

So in a sense, a lot of the pipeline people build around Transformers, tokenizers, patching in vision, learned audio codecs, is doing the job of chunking raw data into meaningful units so attention can operate well. That works, but it's somewhat handcrafted and brittle, and tokenization in particular has well-known failure modes.

Where I'd like to see things go, and part of what motivates our work, is models that can learn these abstractions themselves, operating closer to raw data and dynamically figuring out how to chunk it into meaningful units, possibly hierarchically. Then you can imagine hybrid designs where compressive, recurrent-style layers handle the low-level, high-resolution data, and attention-like mechanisms operate once you've gotten to a more abstract, semantic level. So rather than asking which architecture is better overall, I think the more useful question is which one fits the resolution and the semantic density of the data you're working with.

r001.rationale: The response says attention works well when each token is semantically meaningful and gives words as units that make sensible comparisons.

r002.rationale: It contrasts meaningful words with low-level units that carry little meaning, and says to choose architecture based on the data’s resolution and semantic density—whether comparisons between units make sense.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and I think it actually gets at something pretty fundamental about why Transformers work the way they do and where their limitations are.

The way I'd frame it is that attention is a mechanism that works best on data that's already been compressed into meaningful units. If you look at where Transformers have been most successful, it's on tokenized text, where each token carries a lot of semantic content. And that's not an accident. Attention is essentially doing a lookup over a set of discrete elements, and it's quadratic in the number of elements, so you really want each element to be information-dense. You want to be operating at the level of, you know, words or subwords, not individual characters or bytes.

And I think the tokenizer is kind of an underappreciated part of the pipeline here. People treat it as this preprocessing step, but it's doing a lot of heavy lifting. It's compressing the raw data into a representation where attention is efficient and where the inductive biases of the Transformer actually match the structure of the data. If you try to run a Transformer directly on raw bytes, or on raw audio samples, or on DNA at base-pair resolution, it tends to do much worse, and part of that is just the sequence length, but part of it is that attention isn't really the right operation for data where the individual elements are low-information and the meaningful structure is spread out over many of them.

So in my mind, the question of what level of representation to use is really intertwined with the question of what architecture to use. I'd argue that state space models, or recurrent-style models more generally, are better suited to the raw, high-resolution end of things. They're processing data sequentially, compressing it into a state, and they're naturally good at building up those higher-level units from fine-grained inputs. And then once you're at that higher level of abstraction, attention becomes a lot more compelling, because now you have these dense units that you want to be able to retrieve precisely and compare against each other.

That's actually the intuition behind a lot of the hybrid work, and also behind things like learning the tokenization end to end instead of having a fixed handcrafted tokenizer. The idea is that the model itself should figure out what the right units are, and different layers or different components can operate at different granularities. I think the current setup, where we have a fixed tokenizer bolted onto a uniform stack of attention layers, is kind of a local optimum that we've converged on because it works well for text. But if you care about other modalities, or about getting rid of the tokenizer altogether, you probably need to think about the representation level and the architecture together rather than as separate design choices.

r001.rationale: The response says attention works best on information-dense, meaningful units such as words or subwords, which can be retrieved and compared.

r002.rationale: It discusses meaningful units and precise retrieval, but does not propose using whether attending to one unit at a given level makes sense as the decision test.

astra-6.text:
I think of attention as being most useful when the inputs already represent meaningful pieces of information. It lets you compare those pieces and decide which ones are relevant to each other. So the level of representation matters: what exactly are the things that you’re asking attention to relate?

In language, tokens are a fairly natural starting point. They’re not always whole words, but they already have some discrete structure. With something like raw audio, an individual sample doesn’t have that same meaning. You need to aggregate information over time before you get something that looks like a phoneme or a word. Images have a similar issue: you might want to reason about patches or objects rather than individual pixels.

So I wouldn’t necessarily expect the same architecture to be the best choice at every level. You could use a different mechanism to process the low-level signal and build representations, then use attention at a higher level, where selecting and relating information becomes more useful. The interesting question is how to learn that hierarchy, rather than having to specify all of those boundaries by hand.

r001.rationale: The response says attention is most useful when inputs are meaningful pieces that it can compare and relate.

r002.rationale: It asks what units attention should relate and contrasts meaningful tokens or phonemes with raw audio samples, conveying whether an individual unit is a sensible object of attention.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: at what level does it make sense to compare things? Attention is a very natural mechanism when you have a collection of objects or concepts and you want to reason about how they relate to one another. But the raw data doesn’t necessarily come in at that level.

For example, in language, we give the model tokens, which already have some meaningful structure. In an image, an individual pixel is much less meaningful. And with audio, an individual sample is probably not the thing you want to compare to every other sample. You’d like to first build representations that capture something more useful over a local region or a stretch of time.

So I tend to think there’s room for different mechanisms at different levels. You can use something that’s efficient at processing the raw sequence and building up representations, and then use attention once you have representations where those comparisons are useful. The interesting question is how to learn that hierarchy, rather than deciding in advance that every layer should operate in exactly the same way.

r001.rationale: It says attention suits collections of meaningful objects or concepts for reasoning about their relationships, and notes that language tokens already have meaningful structure.

r002.rationale: It frames the choice as asking at what level it makes sense to compare units, then contrasts meaningful tokens with pixels or audio samples that are less suitable units.
